title: Workshop data
text:
Large rasters are not committed. scripts/fetch_data.sh downloads the prepared GRASS project from the repository’s GitHub Release. This folder holds the area of interest, the source lists, and the provenance record.


Humbug Creek, HUC12 180102060801, Siskiyou County, California (95.7 km2). The creek burned at high severity in the 2022 McKinney Fire (ignition 2022-07-29). On 2022-08-02 a monsoonal storm cell dropped roughly 4 in of rain on the burn scar. A fire control line follows the creek, so unburned terrain sits next to burned channels.

aoi/HumbugCreek.geojson: HUC12 boundary from the Watershed Boundary Dataset, EPSG:4269.
aoi/focal.geojson: the workshop region, the bbox in Tim Bailey’s OpenTopography link (-122.7530, 41.7727, -122.7173, 41.7922). About 3.0 x 2.2 km at 1 m, all inside B22 tile x52y463. The full HUC12 is the optional extension.
Fire perimeter: MTBS McKinney Fire, CA4183012289520220729 (Extended assessment, post-fire scene 2023-08-15), fetched from the USFS EDW MTBS map service by scripts/prepare_data.py.




Collection dates come from the 3DEP WESM index and the OpenTopography catalog, checked 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-15.

The 2022 collection came 6 to 12 weeks after the storm and before the winter rains, so it records the immediate rain-on-fire response.
The epochs use different NAD83 realizations and different geoid models. That difference is part of the lesson on co-registration. Do not hide it in preprocessing.

Both the 2013 file and the USGS 1 m tiles declare EPSG:26910 in their headers, so the realization is only in the collection metadata. The GRASS project uses EPSG:26910 and nothing is reprojected on import.
Treating the 2013 data as NAD83(1986) and transforming to NAD83(2011) moves a point at the site by 0.20 m east and 0.55 m north with the NADCON5 grids, and by 0 m when PROJ cannot reach them. Reprojecting would make the result depend on network access.
GEOID18 minus GEOID12B undulation across the focal region is -0.021 to -0.027 m, so 2022 heights read 2 to 3 cm higher for the same ellipsoid height. GEOID12B stands in for GEOID12A here. NGS documents GEOID12B as identical to GEOID12A except in Puerto Rico (GEOID12B technical details).




OpenTopography distributes the 2013 USFS DTM (raster ID OTSDEM.122022.26910.2, https://doi.org/10.5069/G9FJ2F12) only after you sign in, and it is not in the public bulk buckets. Download it once for the focal region and pass it to scripts/prepare_data.py --dtm2013. Participants get the clipped copy from the release.
The download box in EPSG:26910 is the focal region plus the 100 m clip buffer: xmin 520423, ymin 4624467, xmax 523597, ymax 4626838. Choose GeoTIFF output with the bare-earth and highest-hit layers, then pass output_be.tif as --dtm2013 and output_hh.tif as --dsm2013. Highest hit minus bare earth gives pre-fire canopy height for part 02. Cite the dataset as listed under References.
The delivered 2013 grid starts at 520422.29, 4626838.83, so its cells sit 0.29 m east and 0.17 m south of the whole-meter grid the 2022 data and the focal region use. r.import keeps that grid because the CRS already matches. Notebook 01 resamples the 2013 DTM onto the region with r.resamp.interp (bilinear). Reading the native grid on the region instead takes the nearest cell, which shifts the surface by that offset and changes the DoD by up to 2 m on steep slopes.




The 2010 legacy collection does not cover the focal region, so the noise baseline comes from stable unburned ground across the control line. About 15 percent of the focal region is unburned.




dnbr and burn_severity in PERMANENT (10 m) come from two Sentinel-2 L2A scenes on Element84 Earth Search, imported with t.stac.item by scripts/prepare_data.py:

Pre-fire: S2B_10TEM_20220721_0_L2A, eight days before ignition.
Post-fire: S2B_10TEM_20220909_0_L2A, after the 2022-08-02 storm and five days before the 2022 lidar collection began.

B12 is natively 20 m, so NBR has an effective resolution of 20 m resampled to 10 m. NBR is (B08 - B12) / (B08 + B12) on reflectance, and dnbr is 1000 x (NBR pre - NBR post) minus its median outside the fire perimeter (2.4).
Reflectance is DN x 1e-4. The Earth Search items list a raster:bands offset of -0.1 and set earthsearch:boa_offset_applied: true, and the pixels already have the processing baseline 04.00 offset removed. Applying -0.1 again pushes 20% of pre-fire cells to near-zero reflectance and moves the unburned median dNBR to -25; without it the unburned median is +2.
The classes use the dNBR thresholds MTBS published for this fire (CA4183012289520220729): increased greenness below -150, unburned to low below 35, low below 300, moderate below 530, high from 530. MTBS derived them from a Landsat extended assessment (post-fire scene 2023-08-15), so they approximate classes for this Sentinel-2 initial assessment.
The build falls back to a local perimeter (--perimeter) when the USFS MTBS service is unavailable.



s2_pre_red, s2_pre_green, s2_pre_blue and the matching s2_post_* rasters in PERMANENT are the 10 m red, green, and blue bands (B04, B03, B02) of the same two Sentinel-2 scenes, as reflectance x 10000. Every band of both dates has the same linear color table, black at 0 and white at 0.2 reflectance, so d.rgb shows both dates on one scale. The 98th percentile of the post-fire red band is 0.2.
Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2022.



nhd_flowlines in PERMANENT holds the USGS National Hydrography Dataset large-scale flowlines over the HUC12 bounding box, with gnis_name, ftype, fcode, and lengthkm. scripts/prepare_data.py fetches them from the NHD map service (layer 6) and keeps the GeoJSON in raw/nhd_flowlines.geojson. The build falls back to a local copy (--flowlines) when the service is unavailable. The notebooks still derive channels from the 2022 DTM for the analysis. The NHD lines are for orientation.

title: Geohazard Change Detection with GRASS
text:
The storm of 2 August 2022
Four days after ignition, monsoonal moisture built a convective thunderstorm over the active fire. It rained hard from 17:30 to 20:30.

Rainfall rates above 200 mm/h and more than 100 mm in 3 hours over the Humbug and Vesa Creek watersheds
A 15-minute intensity of 100 mm/h there has a recurrence interval of more than 1000 years
The storm hit Humbug Creek first and set off sediment-laden flooding
Rill and gully erosion on burned hillslopes, debris flows that scoured channels, and debris fans in lower-gradient reaches

Curtis, J.A., et al., 2025. 2022 McKinney rain-on-wildfire event, dissolved oxygen sags, and a fish kill on the Klamath River, California. Scientific Reports 15, 24668. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-08179-9

title: Geohazard Change Detection with GRASS
text:
A cascading hazard
Each step set up the next one.

Fire, 29 July. 83% of the burned area was moderate to high severity.
Storm, 2 August. The trigger. More than 100 mm in 3 hours exceeded what the fire-affected soils could absorb.
Debris flows and channel change. Rill and gully erosion, scoured channels, and debris fans. This is what the DoD measures.
Downstream impacts. Sediment-laden flooding reached the Klamath River. Dissolved oxygen fell to zero for 5.25 hours 71 km downstream, and fish died along 95 km of the river.

Curtis et al. (2025).

Source of error

The same two DEMs, differenced two ways.

Bilinear resampling onto the region

title: Geohazard Change Detection with GRASS
text:
Level of detection

0.149 m

The smallest change we will call real, at 95% confidence.

LoD = 1.96 x NMAD of the DoD on stable ground
Error grows with slope, from an NMAD of 6 cm below 10 degrees to 11 cm above 40 degrees
About 11% of stable cells pass a nominal 95% limit, so the limit is optimistic
Calibrated so that 5% of stable cells pass, the multiplier is 2.9 instead of 1.96, and net lowering drops by about 40%

title: 04. Products for emergency management
text:
Parts 01 to 03 produced a DoD we trust to about 15 cm, and sig_slope, the change in that DoD that clears a slope-based level of detection. Part 03 also showed that this 95% level is optimistic, with about 11% of stable cells passing instead of 5%, so some of the smallest significant change here is noise. The calibrated LoD in part 03 keeps about 40% less net lowering. In this part we summarize that change the way a response team would ask about it: by burn severity, by subwatershed, and in channels versus hillslopes, and then run a 10 m screening pass that combines topographic and spectral change.
import io

from workshop_utils import gj, gs, rounded, start

tools, session = start(
    "04",
    required=["dod_debiased", "sig_slope", "dtm_2022", "stream_distance", "burned"],
)
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="sig_lowering = if(sig_slope < 0, sig_slope, null())")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="sig_raising = if(sig_slope > 0, sig_slope, null())")

Part 04 ready in mapset workshop

title: 04. Products for emergency management
text:
Burn severity
burn_severity comes from Sentinel-2 dNBR between 21 July and 9 September 2022, classed with the thresholds MTBS published for this fire. NBR uses the 20 m shortwave infrared band resampled to 10 m, and the thresholds come from a Landsat assessment, so treat the classes as approximate. See data/README.md for the details.

severity_map = gj.Map(width=700)
severity_map.d_shade(shade="dtm_2022_relief", color="burn_severity@PERMANENT")
severity_map.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
)
severity_map.d_legend(
    raster="burn_severity@PERMANENT",
    title="Burn severity",
    at=(5, 35, 2, 5),
    fontsize=11,
    flags="b",
)
severity_map.show()

title: 04. Products for emergency management
04. Products for emergency management
text:
Change by subwatershed
A response team allocates by drainage. Split the region into subwatersheds of at least 20 ha with r.watershed and total the significant change in each. Subwatersheds cut by the edge of the region only carry the part inside it.

tools.r_watershed(elevation="dtm_2022", threshold=200_000, basin="basins", flags="a")
tools.r_to_vect(input="basins", output="basins", type="area", flags="s")
tools.r_stats_zonal(base="basins", cover="sig_slope", method="sum", output="basin_net")
# Red for net lowering, blue for net raising, symmetric about zero.
stats = tools.r_univar(map="basin_net", format="json")
extreme = max(abs(stats["min"]), abs(stats["max"]))
tools.r_colors(
    map="basin_net",
    rules=io.StringIO(f"{-extreme} 178:24:43\n0 247:247:247\n{extreme} 33:102:172\n"),
)

net = sorted(
    (
        (z["zone"], z["sum"], z["n"])
        for z in tools.r_univar(map="sig_slope", zones="basins", format="json")
    ),
    key=lambda item: item[1],
)
print("Subwatersheds with the most net lowering:")
for zone, total, _ in net[:5]:
    print(f"  basin {zone:>5}: {rounded(total):>+12,.0f} m3")

Subwatersheds with the most net lowering:
  basin    56:      -78,000 m3
  basin    82:      -73,000 m3
  basin    42:      -55,000 m3
  basin    46:      -44,000 m3
  basin    76:      -34,000 m3



basin_map = gj.Map(width=700)
basin_map.d_shade(shade="dtm_2022_relief", color="basin_net")
basin_map.d_vect(map="basins", fill_color="none", color="white", width=1)
basin_map.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
)
basin_map.d_legend(
    raster="basin_net", title="Net change (m3)", at=(5, 40, 2, 5), flags="b"
)
basin_map.show()

title: 04. Products for emergency management
text:
Channels and hillslopes
Part 02 kept channels out of the stable mask. Here they are the point: compare the change within 10 m of a channel with the change on the hillslopes.

tools.r_category(

raising = zonal_sums("sig_raising", "landform")
area = {
    z["zone"]: z["n"]
    for z in tools.r_univar(map="dod_debiased", zones="landform", format="json")
}
print(f"{'':10}{'area ha':>9}{'lowering m3':>13}{'raising m3':>12}{'net m3/ha':>11}")
for zone in (1, 2):
    label = lowering[zone][0]
    hectares = area[zone] / 10_000
    low, rise = lowering[zone][1], raising[zone][1]
    print(
        f"{label:10}{hectares:>9.1f}{rounded(low):>13,.0f}{rounded(rise):>12,.0f}"

hillslope     547.7     -380,000      35,000       -620


The net change per hectare is about the same in channels and on hillslopes, but channels both lost and gained more. They lost about 1,000 m3 per hectare against about 690 on the hillslopes, and gained about six times as much per hectare, where material moving off the slopes settled.

title: 04. Products for emergency management
text:
A 10 m screening pass
r.dem.screen is a coarse first pass for directing field crews. It flags topographic change where the DoD exceeds a threshold and spectral change where vegetation was lost, and ranks cells with both highest. Here the spectral change is the NBR change, post minus pre, so loss is negative.

with gs.RegionManager(region="focal@PERMANENT", res=10, flags="a"):
    tools.r_resamp_stats(input="dod_debiased", output="dod_10m", method="average")
    tools.r_mapcalc(expression="nbr_change = -dnbr@PERMANENT / 1000.0")
    tools.r_dem_screen(
        dod="dod_10m",
        spectral_change="nbr_change",
        output="screen",
        topo_threshold=0.25,
        spectral_threshold=-0.15,
    )
    print(tools.r_stats(input="screen", flags="lcpn").text)

0 No significant change 14663 22.75%
1 Spectral change (vegetation damage) 46213 71.71%
2 Topographic change (geomorphic) 312 0.48%
3 Topo + Spectral (highest priority) 3261 5.06%


Averaging to 10 m smooths the DoD, so a 10 m cell rarely moves as much as its steepest 1 m cells. At 0.5 m almost no cells pass; at 0.25 m about 5% show both topographic and spectral change, a workable list for a field crew. Spectral change alone covers most of the burn scar, so the combined class is what narrows the search.

screen_map = gj.Map(width=700)
screen_map.d_shade(shade="dtm_2022_relief", color="screen")
screen_map.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
)
screen_map.d_legend(
    raster="screen", title="Screening", at=(5, 35, 2, 5), fontsize=11, flags="b"
)
screen_map.show()








With roads or other infrastructure as a vector map, the r.dem.screen options infrastructure= and hazard_output= mark where change meets assets.

title: 04. Products for emergency management
text:
In context
Curtis et al. (2025) describe the 2 August 2022 storm over the burn scar: rainfall rates above 200 mm/h and 3-hour totals above 100 mm, highest in Humbug Creek, followed by rill and gully erosion and debris flows that scoured channels and left fans in lower reaches. USGS post-fire debris-flow models predicted 57,000 to 3,676,000 m3 of debris-flow volume for Humbug Creek, for a design storm with a 15-minute intensity of 40 mm/h. The observed rainfall rates were well above that.
Our volumes measure something different. They cover 6.4 km2 of the watershed, they include all surface lowering above the level of detection, not only sediment that left, and they span September 2013 to fall 2022, not just the storm. The DoD tells you where the surface changed and by how much. Attributing that change to the storm, to the fire, or to sediment delivery takes the field evidence and additional dates.
Curtis, J.A., et al., 2025. 2022 McKinney rain-on-wildfire event, dissolved oxygen sags, and a fish kill on the Klamath River, California. Scientific Reports 15, 24668. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-08179-9

title: 02. Co-registration and bias
text:
Part 01 ended with a naive DoD that reads about 10 cm high on ground that did not burn, with a color pattern on the hillslopes that follows aspect. In this part we measure that error on stable ground, remove the offset between the two lidar collections with r.dem.nk, and check whether pre-fire vegetation leaves a bias worth correcting.
import io
import json

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from workshop_utils import RAW, garray, gj, stable_stats, start

tools, session = start(
    "02", required=["dtm_2013", "dtm_2022", "dod_naive", "burned", "slope_2013"]
)

Part 02 ready in mapset workshop

title: 02. Co-registration and bias
text:
Stable ground
Every correction in this part is estimated on ground we expect did not change between 2013 and 2022. Here that means cells that are outside the fire perimeter, sloped between 2 and 45 degrees, and more than 10 m from a channel, since channels carry real deposition and scour.

tools.r_watershed(elevation="dtm_2022", threshold=10000, stream="streams", flags="a")
tools.r_grow_distance(input="streams", distance="stream_distance")
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression=(
        "stable = if(burned == 0 && slope_2013 >= 2 && slope_2013 <= 45 "
        "&& stream_distance > 10, 1, null())"
    )
)

tools.r_mapcalc(expression="channels = if(isnull(streams), null(), 1)")
tools.r_colors(map="channels", rules=io.StringIO("1 30:100:255\n"))
tools.r_colors(map="stable", rules=io.StringIO("1 255:200:0\n"))

n_stable = tools.r_univar(map="stable", format="json")["n"]
n_region = tools.g_region(flags="p", format="json")["cells"]
print(f"Stable cells: {n_stable} ({100 * n_stable / n_region:.1f}% of the region)")

Stable cells: 782568 (12.1% of the region)



stable_map = gj.Map(width=700)
stable_map.d_rast(map="dtm_2022_relief")
stable_map.d_rast(map="stable")
stable_map.d_rast(map="channels")
stable_map.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="red", width=2
)
stable_map.show()








Now the numbers to beat. The median is the systematic offset and the NMAD (normalized median absolute deviation) is the noise, both measured where the true change should be zero.

before = stable_stats(tools, "dod_naive", "stable")
print(
    f"Naive DoD on stable ground: median {before['median']:+.3f} m, NMAD {before['nmad']:.3f} m"
)

Naive DoD on stable ground: median +0.097 m, NMAD 0.078 m

title: 02. Co-registration and bias
text:
Horizontal and vertical offset
A horizontal shift between two DEMs shows up as an elevation error that depends on slope and aspect. r.dem.nk fits the Nuth and Kaab (2011) model to that pattern on the stable cells and returns the shift. We align the 2013 DTM to the 2022 reference, since the 2022 collection is the newer, higher-specification survey.

# sfm= is the surface to move, here the 2013 lidar DTM, and lidar= is the
# reference it is aligned to.
tools.r_dem_nk(
    sfm="dtm_2013",
    lidar="dtm_2022",
    stable_mask="stable",
    output="dtm_2013_nk",
    transform_output="nk_transform.txt",
)

offsets = {}
with open("nk_transform.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        if "=" in line:
            key, value = line.strip().split("=")
            offsets[key] = float(value)
horizontal = np.hypot(offsets["dx"], offsets["dy"])
print(
    f"dx {offsets['dx']:+.3f} m, dy {offsets['dy']:+.3f} m, dz {offsets['dz']:+.3f} m"
)
print(f"Horizontal shift: {horizontal:.2f} m")

dx -0.036 m, dy -0.039 m, dz -0.086 m
Horizontal shift: 0.05 m


The horizontal shift is about 5 cm, a twentieth of a cell. In a nearest-cell DoD the same fit finds about 0.35 m, almost all of it the grid offset that part 01 resampled away. The vertical offset of about 9 cm is larger than the 2 to 3 cm geoid difference from part 01, so the geoid change explains only part of it. An iterative closest point fit with r.dem.icp on the same mask points the same way, with about 8 cm horizontal and 10 cm vertical. The two methods differ by about 3 cm, close to the size of the horizontal shift itself, so the vertical offset is well resolved and the horizontal one is small and uncertain.
The small shift also settles the datum question from part 01. If the 2013 data were on the original NAD83, the fit would find a shift near 0.6 m. It finds 5 cm, so applying the NADCON5 grid shift would have added error, not removed it.
Difference the aligned 2013 DTM against 2022 with r.dem.dod. Both DoDs use range=1 so they share one color scale.

tools.r_dem_dod(dem="dtm_2022", reference="dtm_2013_nk", output="dod_nk", range=1)

after = stable_stats(tools, "dod_nk", "stable")
print(f"{'':12}{'median':>10}{'NMAD':>10}")
for label, stats in (("naive", before), ("r.dem.nk", after)):
    print(f"{label:12}{stats['median']:>+10.3f}{stats['nmad']:>10.3f}")

                median      NMAD
naive           +0.097     0.078
r.dem.nk        +0.009     0.075



for name in ("dod_naive", "dod_nk"):
    dod_map = gj.Map(width=500)
    dod_map.d_shade(shade="dtm_2022_relief", color=name)
    dod_map.d_vect(
        map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
    )
    dod_map.show()
# One legend for both maps.
legend = gj.Map(width=1000, height=110)
legend.d_legend(
    raster="dod_nk",
    title="DoD (m)",
    range=(-1, 1),
    at=(35, 65, 5, 95),
    flags="st",
    fontsize=14,
    title_fontsize=16,
)
legend.show()











(a) Naive DoD











(b) After r.dem.nk













(c) Legend for both maps







Figure 1: The DoD before and after co-registration, on one color scale




The median drops from about +0.10 to +0.01 m, while the NMAD barely moves. A vertical offset moves every cell by the same amount, and the horizontal shift is small, so removing them recenters the error without narrowing it.
All of the stable ground sits in the eastern part of the region, and much of the burn lies west of it. The offsets are fit there and applied everywhere. A tilt between the two surveys would not show up in this fit and would grow with distance from the stable ground, so keep that in mind when reading the volumes in parts 03 and 04.
To check the horizontal part, plot the stable-ground error divided by the tangent of slope against aspect. A horizontal shift traces a cosine in this plot, and a vertical offset lifts the whole curve.

tools.r_slope_aspect(
    elevation="dtm_2022", slope="slope_2022", aspect="aspect_2022", flags="n"
)
slope = garray.array("slope_2022", null=np.nan)
aspect = garray.array("aspect_2022", null=np.nan)
# Read the integer mask as float so null cells become NaN.
stable_cells = garray.array("stable", dtype=np.float64, null=np.nan)
on_stable = ~np.isnan(stable_cells) & (slope >= 5)

edges = np.arange(0, 361, 15)
centers = edges[:-1] + 7.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
for name, label in (("dod_naive", "naive"), ("dod_nk", "after r.dem.nk")):
    ratio = garray.array(name, null=np.nan) / np.tan(np.radians(slope))
    medians = [
        np.nanmedian(ratio[on_stable & (aspect >= lo) & (aspect < hi)])
        for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:])
    ]
    ax.plot(centers, medians, marker="o", label=label)
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Aspect (degrees from north)")
ax.set_ylabel("DoD / tan(slope) (m)")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 361, 45))
ax.legend()
plt.show()








Before co-registration the curve sits high, which is the vertical offset, with a gentle cosine on top. After r.dem.nk it sits near zero with a few centimeters of wiggle left.

title: 02. Co-registration and bias
text:
Vegetation
Pre-fire canopy can bias a DTM. Dense canopy leaves fewer ground returns, so the 2013 bare-earth surface is interpolated over larger gaps than the 2022 surface flown after the fire. The 2013 highest-hit surface minus the bare-earth surface gives canopy height. A few highest-hit returns are blunders hundreds of meters up, so heights above 70 m are dropped.

tools.r_import(
    input=str(RAW / "usfs_2013_dsm.tif"), output="dsm_2013_native", extent="region"
)
# The highest-hit surface sits on its own offset grid, so resample it like the DTM.
tools.r_resamp_interp(input="dsm_2013_native", output="dsm_2013", method="bilinear")
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression=(
        "canopy_2013 = if(dsm_2013 - dtm_2013 > 70, null(), "
        "max(dsm_2013 - dtm_2013, 0))"
    )
)
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="forest = if(canopy_2013 > 2, 1, null())")
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="stable_forest = if(!isnull(stable) && !isnull(forest), 1, null())"
)
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="stable_open = if(!isnull(stable) && isnull(forest), 1, null())"
)
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="burned_forest = if(burned == 1 && !isnull(forest), 1, null())"
)

for label, mask in (
    ("stable forest", "stable_forest"),
    ("stable open", "stable_open"),
    ("burned forest", "burned_forest"),
):
    stats = stable_stats(tools, "dod_nk", mask)
    print(
        f"{label:14} median {stats['median']:+.3f} m, NMAD {stats['nmad']:.3f} m, cells {stats['n']}"
    )

stable forest  median -0.005 m, NMAD 0.085 m, cells 306818
stable open    median +0.017 m, NMAD 0.066 m, cells 475750
burned forest  median -0.115 m, NMAD 0.111 m, cells 2349146


On stable ground, forest and open cells differ by about 2 cm. Burned forest reads about 12 cm lower, which is change we want to keep.
r.dem.bias method=forest estimates a local median under a canopy mask and subtracts it. Applied to burned forest, it would remove that 12 cm along with any bias, because a local median cannot tell the two apart. method=regression instead fits the bias to terrain and canopy predictors on stable ground only and predicts it everywhere, which keeps real change out of the fit.

tools.r_dem_bias(
    dod="dod_nk",
    output="dod_debiased",
    method="regression",
    predictors="slope_2013,canopy_2013",
    stable_mask="stable",
    bias_field="bias_regression",
    fit_json="bias_fit.json",
)

with open("bias_fit.json") as f:
    fit = json.load(f)
print("Intercept:", round(fit["intercept"], 4))
for name, value in fit["coefficients"].items():
    print(f"{name:12} {value:+.4f} m per standard deviation")

debiased = stable_stats(tools, "dod_debiased", "stable")
print(
    f"Stable ground after regression: median {debiased['median']:+.3f} m, NMAD {debiased['nmad']:.3f} m"
)

Intercept: 0.0056
slope_2013   -0.0112 m per standard deviation
canopy_2013  +0.0057 m per standard deviation
Stable ground after regression: median +0.004 m, NMAD 0.076 m


The regression changes the stable-ground median by millimeters. After co-registration there is little vegetation bias left to remove at this site, and measuring it first is how you know. Part 03 starts from dod_debiased.

Turn significant change into volumes and post-event change maps by burn severity and subwatershed, and export them for desktop GIS.

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
We start with two lidar DTMs of the focal region. One was flown in September 2013. The other was flown in fall 2022, six to twelve weeks after the McKinney Fire and the August 2 storm. By the end of this part both epochs are in GRASS, registered in a space-time raster dataset, and differenced into a first DEM of Difference (DoD). The rest of the workshop is about how far to trust it.
import io
import os
import subprocess

from workshop_utils import RAW, Tools, gj, gs, stable_stats, start

tools, session = start("01")

Part 01 ready in mapset workshop

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
Coordinate reference systems and datums
Both files report the same coordinate reference system (CRS).

epochs = {
    "dtm_2013_native": RAW / "usfs_2013_dtm.tif",
    "dtm_2022": RAW / "usgs_2022_dtm.tif",
}
for name, path in epochs.items():
    crs = tools.g_proj(flags="p", georef=str(path), format="projjson")
    print(f"{name}: {crs['name']}")

dtm_2013_native: NAD83 / UTM zone 10N
dtm_2022: NAD83 / UTM zone 10N


The collection metadata tells a different story.



Epoch
Horizontal datum
Vertical datum




2013, USFS
NAD83
NAVD88, GEOID12A


2022, USGS 3DEP
NAD83(2011)
NAVD88, GEOID18



The file headers do not record the NAD83 realization. If we tell PROJ the 2013 file is the original NAD83 and ask for NAD83(2011), it applies the NADCON5 grid shift. Without the grid it silently applies none.

point = "522000 4625000 0\n"
for network in ("OFF", "ON"):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["cs2cs", "-d", "3", "EPSG:26910", "EPSG:6339"],
        input=point,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        env={**os.environ, "PROJ_NETWORK": network},
    ).stdout.split()
    print(f"PROJ_NETWORK={network}: 522000 4625000 -> {out[0]} {out[1]}")

PROJ_NETWORK=OFF: 522000 4625000 -> 522000.000 4625000.000
PROJ_NETWORK=ON: 522000 4625000 -> 522000.202 4625000.552


With the grid, that point moves about 0.6 m. The geoid models differ too. Here GEOID18 sits 2 to 3 cm below GEOID12A (compared with GEOID12B, which NGS documents as identical to GEOID12A outside Puerto Rico), so the same ground reads 2 to 3 cm higher in 2022 before anything has changed.
We do not resolve either offset by relabeling files. The project uses EPSG:26910, the CRS both files declare, so nothing is reprojected on import and the result does not depend on whether PROJ can reach its grids. Part 02 measures the remaining horizontal and vertical offset on stable ground instead.

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
Import both epochs
The computational region is the focal area at 1 m. r.import clips each file to the region. Both files already use the project CRS, so nothing is reprojected, and each epoch keeps the grid it was delivered on.

for name, path in epochs.items():
    tools.r_import(
        input=str(path),
        output=name,
        extent="region",
        overwrite=True,
    )

region = gs.region()
for name in epochs:
    info = gs.raster_info(name)
    dx = (info["west"] - region["w"] + 0.5) % region["ewres"] - 0.5
    dy = (info["north"] - region["n"] + 0.5) % region["nsres"] - 0.5
    print(f"{name}: offset from the region grid {dx:+.3f} m east, {dy:+.3f} m north")

dtm_2013_native: offset from the region grid +0.290 m east, -0.170 m north
dtm_2022: offset from the region grid -0.000 m east, +0.000 m north


The 2022 grid sits on the region grid. The 2013 grid is offset by about a third of a cell. Any tool that reads the 2013 DTM on this region takes the nearest 2013 cell, which moves the whole surface by that offset. Resample it onto the region with bilinear interpolation and use that as the working 2013 DTM.

tools.r_resamp_interp(input="dtm_2013_native", output="dtm_2013", method="bilinear")
for name in ("dtm_2013", "dtm_2022"):
    tools.r_relief(input=name, output=f"{name}_relief", overwrite=True)


tools.v_to_rast(
    input="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT",
    output="burned_area",
    use="val",
    value=1,
    overwrite=True,
)
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="burned = if(isnull(burned_area), 0, 1)", overwrite=True)
tools.r_category(
    map="burned", separator=":", rules=io.StringIO("0:unburned\n1:burned\n")
)

# Color the burned ground by elevation and leave the unburned ground gray.
tools.r_colors(map="dtm_2022", color="elevation")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="dtm_2022_burned = if(burned == 1, dtm_2022, null())")
tools.r_colors(map="dtm_2022_burned", raster="dtm_2022")

fire = gj.Map(width=700)
fire.d_rast(map="dtm_2022_relief")
fire.d_shade(shade="dtm_2022_relief", color="dtm_2022_burned")
fire.d_vect(map="nhd_flowlines@PERMANENT", color="0:92:230", width=1)
fire.d_vect(map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="red", width=2)
fire.d_legend(
    raster="dtm_2022", title="Elevation 2022 (m)", at=(5, 40, 2, 5), flags="b"
)
fire.show()








The red line is the MTBS fire perimeter. Ground inside it, which burned, is colored by elevation. Ground outside it is gray. The blue lines are the mapped streams from the USGS National Hydrography Dataset (NHD). The fire control line follows Humbug Creek, so part of this region did not burn. That unburned ground is what we use to measure error.

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
The temporal framework
With two epochs a time series sounds like overkill. It stops being overkill the first time you add a third collection, and it keeps the acquisition dates attached to the data. Each epoch is registered with its collection window as a time interval.

# GRASS intervals end exclusively, so each end date is the day after the last flight.
with open("epochs.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("dtm_2013|2013-09-04|2013-09-08\n")
    f.write("dtm_2022|2022-09-14|2022-10-29\n")

tools.t_create(
    output="dtm",
    type="strds",
    temporaltype="absolute",
    title="Humbug Creek lidar DTMs",
    description="Bare-earth DTMs, 1 m, focal region",
    overwrite=True,
)
tools.t_register(input="dtm", type="raster", file="epochs.txt", overwrite=True)
print(tools.t_rast_list(input="dtm", columns="name,start_time,end_time").text)

name|start_time|end_time
dtm_2013|2013-09-04 00:00:00|2013-09-08 00:00:00
dtm_2022|2022-09-14 00:00:00|2022-10-29 00:00:00

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
A naive DoD
Subtract the earlier epoch from the later one with r.dem.dod, pulling the map names from the dataset in time order. Negative values are surface lowering (erosion), positive values are surface raising (deposition). range=1 fixes the color scale at plus or minus 1 m so later DoDs compare with this one.

names = tools.t_rast_list(
    input="dtm", columns="name", order="start_time", flags="u"
).text.split()
before, after = names[0], names[-1]
tools.r_dem_dod(dem=after, reference=before, output="dod_naive", range=1)
print(f"dod_naive = {after} - {before}")

dod_naive = dtm_2022 - dtm_2013



dod = gj.Map(width=700)
dod.d_shade(shade="dtm_2022_relief", color="dod_naive")
dod.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
)
dod.d_legend(
    raster="dod_naive", title="DoD (m)", range=(-1, 1), at=(5, 40, 2, 5), flags="b"
)
dod.show()









What nearest-cell sampling does
r.mapcalc reads every input on the region grid and takes the nearest cell. Give it the native 2013 grid and compare with the resampled DoD. r.dem.dod run on the same native grid resamples it and prints a warning with the offset.

# Keep the warning text so it shows in the notebook.
result = Tools(capture_stderr=True, consistent_return_value=True).r_dem_dod(
    dem="dtm_2022", reference="dtm_2013_native", output="dod_resampled", range=1
)
print(result.stderr.strip())
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="dod_nearest = dtm_2022 - dtm_2013_native")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="nearest_error = dod_nearest - dod_naive")
error = tools.r_univar(map="nearest_error", format="json")
print(
    f"Nearest-cell DoD minus resampled DoD: min {error['min']:+.2f} m, "
    f"max {error['max']:+.2f} m, std {error['stddev']:.3f} m"
)

WARNING: Raster map <dtm_2013_native> is not aligned with the computational
         region (resolution 1 x 1, origin offset 0.290, -0.170). Resampling
         with bilinear interpolation.
Nearest-cell DoD minus resampled DoD: min -2.18 m, max +2.25 m, std 0.108 m


Two patterns stand out. Humbug Creek and the side channels are blue, which is deposition after the storm. On the hillslopes the color shifts with the direction a slope faces, which is what a horizontal offset between the epochs would produce. Part 02 measures how much of that offset is real.

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
Burned and unburned ground
If the DoD were all real change, unburned ground would average close to zero. Compare the two.

stats = tools.r_univar(map="dod_naive", zones="burned", flags="e", format="json")
for zone in stats:
    print(
        f"{zone['zone_label']:>9}: mean {zone['mean']:+.3f} m, median {zone['median']:+.3f} m, "
        f"std {zone['stddev']:.3f} m, cells {zone['n']}"
    )

 unburned: mean +0.094 m, median +0.098 m, std 0.167 m, cells 952308
   burned: mean -0.017 m, median -0.013 m, std 0.160 m, cells 5504246


Write down the unburned mean and standard deviation. A nonzero mean on ground that did not burn is systematic error, which includes the datum offsets above. The spread is noise. Part 02 removes the first and part 03 turns the second into a level of detection.

title: 01. Data, datums, and the temporal framework
text:
Your turn
Error on steep slopes is often larger because a small horizontal offset turns into a large vertical one. Split the unburned ground into slope classes and compare the DoD spread two ways: the standard deviation, and the NMAD (normalized median absolute deviation), a spread estimate that a few large outliers cannot pull. Change breaks and see how the numbers move.

tools.r_slope_aspect(elevation="dtm_2013", slope="slope_2013", overwrite=True)

# Slope class breaks in degrees. Try other breaks, then rerun this cell and the next.
breaks = [0, 15, 30, 90]
labels = {
    n: f"{lo}-{hi} deg" for n, (lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(breaks, breaks[1:]), start=1)
}
# Nested if() gives each unburned cell the number of its slope class.
classes = "null()"
for n in sorted(labels, reverse=True):
    classes = f"if(slope_2013 < {breaks[n]}, {n}, {classes})"
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression=f"slope_class = if(burned == 0, {classes}, null())", overwrite=True
)

spread = {
    zone["zone"]: zone
    for zone in tools.r_univar(map="dod_naive", zones="slope_class", format="json")
}
print(f"{'class':>10}{'mean':>9}{'std':>8}{'NMAD':>8}")
for n, label in labels.items():
    tools.r_mapcalc(expression=f"slope_bin = if(slope_class == {n}, 1, null())")
    nmad = stable_stats(tools, "dod_naive", "slope_bin")["nmad"]
    print(
        f"{label:>10}{spread[n]['mean']:>+9.3f}{spread[n]['stddev']:>8.3f}{nmad:>8.3f}"
    )

     class     mean     std    NMAD
  0-15 deg   +0.119   0.205   0.076
 15-30 deg   +0.079   0.145   0.082
 30-90 deg   +0.097   0.157   0.092


Map the slope classes on the unburned ground, colored from light to dark by their mean offset, with the mean in the legend. If the offset were a single vertical shift, every class would have the same mean. Rerun this cell after changing the class breaks.

means = {n: spread[n]["mean"] for n in labels}
tools.r_category(
    map="slope_class",
    separator=":",
    rules=io.StringIO(
        "".join(f"{n}:{labels[n]}, mean {means[n]:+.3f} m\n" for n in labels)
    ),
)
# Light to dark in order of mean offset, for any number of classes.
light, dark = (255, 237, 160), (240, 59, 32)
order = sorted(means, key=means.get)


def shade(rank):
    t = rank / max(len(order) - 1, 1)
    return ":".join(str(round(a + (b - a) * t)) for a, b in zip(light, dark))


color_of = {n: shade(rank) for rank, n in enumerate(order)}
# r.colors needs the rules in ascending category order.
tools.r_colors(
    map="slope_class",
    rules=io.StringIO("".join(f"{n} {color_of[n]}\n" for n in sorted(means))),
)

offsets = gj.Map(width=700)
offsets.d_rast(map="dtm_2013_relief")
offsets.d_shade(shade="dtm_2013_relief", color="slope_class")
offsets.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
)
offsets.d_legend(
    raster="slope_class",
    title="Slope class (unburned)",
    at=(5, 5 + 8 * len(labels), 2, 5),
    fontsize=12,
    title_fontsize=13,
    flags="b",
)
offsets.show()








With the default breaks the class means fall between +0.08 and +0.12 m with no steady trend. Most of the offset is a vertical shift shared by every class. The standard deviation does not grow with slope either, because a small share of large differences dominates it. The NMAD ignores those and does grow with slope, from about 7.6 cm below 15 degrees to about 9.2 cm above 30. Part 03 builds its level of detection on that trend. Rerun the nearest-cell DoD through these classes and the spread between them grows, because the grid offset acts like a horizontal shift. Part 02 separates the vertical offset from what horizontal offset remains.

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
text:
Part 02 left a DoD, dod_debiased, whose stable ground is centered near zero with an NMAD of about 8 cm. In this part we turn that noise into a level of detection (LoD), the smallest change we are willing to call real, and see how the choice of LoD changes the volumes.
import csv

from workshop_utils import Tools, gj, rounded, stable_stats, start

tools, session = start(
    "03", required=["dod_debiased", "stable", "slope_2013", "burned"]
)
# A second Tools instance that keeps message output, for tools that report numbers there.
report = Tools(capture_stderr=True, consistent_return_value=True)
n_region = tools.g_region(flags="p", format="json")["cells"]

Part 03 ready in mapset workshop

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
text:
A single LoD
r.dem.lod method=global estimates the NMAD on stable ground and multiplies it by the normal critical value for the confidence level, 1.96 at 95%.

result = report.r_dem_lod(
    dod="dod_debiased",
    output="lod_global",
    method="global",
    stable_mask="stable",
    confidence=0.95,
)
print(result.stderr.strip())

Estimating NMAD from stable pixels...
Estimated NMAD: 0.0758 m
Global LoD (95% CI):
NMAD: 0.0758 m
sigma: 0.0758 m
z: 1.9600
LoD: 0.1486 m (uniform)

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
section: A local LoD needs stable ground nearby
text:
A local LoD needs stable ground nearby
method=local estimates the NMAD in a moving window instead. With a stable mask, it only defines the LoD where the window reaches stable cells, and it does not extend it beyond them. Our stable ground is the unburned corner of the region.

result = report.r_dem_lod(
    dod="dod_debiased",
    output="lod_local",
    method="local",
    stable_mask="stable",
    window=21,
)
print(result.stderr.strip().splitlines()[0])

Significance domain: 948639 of 6446257 observed cells (14.7%)


A local LoD covers about 15% of the region and almost none of the burn scar, so it cannot test the change we care about here. It works when stable ground is spread through the study area.

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
text:
An LoD from terrain
The NMAD grows with slope (part 01), and slope is known everywhere. Estimate the NMAD of the stable residuals by slope class, then assign each cell the NMAD of its slope class. The error model is fit on stable ground and carried to the burn scar by slope, not by distance.

edges = [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 90]
sigma_by_class = []
print(f"{'slope (deg)':>12}{'median':>10}{'NMAD':>10}{'cells':>10}")
for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
    tools.r_mapcalc(
        expression=f"slope_bin = if(slope_2013 >= {lo} && slope_2013 < {hi}, 1, null())"
    )
    tools.r_mapcalc(
        expression="stable_bin = if(!isnull(stable) && !isnull(slope_bin), 1, null())"
    )
    stats = stable_stats(tools, "dod_debiased", "stable_bin")
    sigma_by_class.append(stats["nmad"])
    print(
        f"{f'{lo}-{hi}':>12}{stats['median']:>+10.3f}{stats['nmad']:>10.3f}{stats['n']:>10}"
    )

# Nested if() assigns each cell the NMAD of its slope class.
expression = "sigma_slope = "
for hi, sigma in zip(edges[1:], sigma_by_class):
    expression += f"if(slope_2013 < {hi}, {sigma}, "
expression += "null()" + ")" * len(sigma_by_class)
tools.r_mapcalc(expression=expression)
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="lod_slope = 1.96 * sigma_slope")

 slope (deg)    median      NMAD     cells
        0-10    +0.008     0.061     88065
       10-20    +0.006     0.067    215487
       20-30    -0.004     0.081    289941
       30-40    +0.011     0.084    170738
       40-90    +0.035     0.107     18335



lod_map = gj.Map(width=700)
lod_map.d_rast(map="lod_slope")
lod_map.d_vect(
    map="mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT", fill_color="none", color="black", width=2
)
lod_map.d_legend(raster="lod_slope", title="LoD (m)", at=(5, 40, 2, 5), flags="b")
lod_map.show()

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
text:
Significant change and volumes
r.dem.change keeps the cells whose change exceeds the LoD, removes isolated significant cells with -n, and writes the volumes. It calls lowering erosion and raising deposition.

def volumes(lod, name):
    tools.r_dem_change(
        dod="dod_debiased",
        lod=lod,
        output_sig=f"sig_{name}",
        volume_csv=f"volumes_{name}.csv",
        flags="n",
    )
    with open(f"volumes_{name}.csv") as f:
        return {row["metric"]: float(row["value_m3"]) for row in csv.DictReader(f)}


results = {
    name: volumes(lod, name)
    for name, lod in (("global", "lod_global"), ("slope", "lod_slope"))
}

# For comparison, the volumes with no LoD at all (1 m cells, so m3 = m * 1 m2).
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="dod_lowering = if(dod_debiased < 0, dod_debiased, null())")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression="dod_raising = if(dod_debiased > 0, dod_debiased, null())")
results["no LoD"] = {
    "erosion": -tools.r_univar(map="dod_lowering", format="json")["sum"],
    "deposition": tools.r_univar(map="dod_raising", format="json")["sum"],
}
results["no LoD"]["net"] = (
    results["no LoD"]["deposition"] - results["no LoD"]["erosion"]
)

print(f"{'':10}{'erosion m3':>14}{'deposition m3':>16}{'net m3':>14}")
for name, v in results.items():

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
section: Check the LoD against stable ground
text:
Check the LoD against stable ground
At 95% confidence, about 5% of stable cells should come out significant by chance. Count them.

for name, lod in (("global", "lod_global"), ("slope", "lod_slope")):
    tools.r_mapcalc(
        expression=f"flagged = if(!isnull(stable) && !isnull(sig_{name}), 1, null())"
    )
    flagged = tools.r_univar(map="flagged", format="json")["n"]

        f"{name:7}: {100 * flagged / tested:.1f}% of stable cells flagged significant"
    )

global : 10.9% of stable cells flagged significant
slope  : 10.8% of stable cells flagged significant


About twice the nominal 5%. The stable residuals have heavier tails than a normal distribution, so an NMAD-based 95% limit is optimistic here. A higher confidence level, or an LoD calibrated so that 5% of stable cells pass, is the honest response.

title: 03. Level of detection and significant change
text:
A calibrated LoD
Find the multiple of the slope-class NMAD that only 5% of stable cells exceed, and use it in place of 1.96.

# Each stable cell's DoD in units of its slope-class NMAD.
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="z_stable = if(!isnull(stable), abs(dod_debiased) / sigma_slope, null())"
)
text = tools.r_quantile(input="z_stable", percentiles=95).text
z_calibrated = float(text.strip().split(":")[-1])
tools.r_mapcalc(expression=f"lod_calibrated = {z_calibrated} * sigma_slope")
results["calibrated"] = volumes("lod_calibrated", "calibrated")

tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="flagged = if(!isnull(stable) && !isnull(sig_calibrated), 1, null())"
)
flagged = tools.r_univar(map="flagged", format="json")["n"]
tested = stable_stats(tools, "lod_calibrated", "stable")["n"]
print(f"Multiplier {z_calibrated:.2f} instead of 1.96")
print(f"{100 * flagged / tested:.1f}% of stable cells flagged significant\n")
print(f"{'':12}{'erosion m3':>14}{'deposition m3':>16}{'net m3':>14}")
for name in ("slope", "calibrated", "no LoD"):
    v = results[name]
    print(
        f"{name:12}{rounded(v['erosion']):>14,.0f}{rounded(v['deposition']):>16,.0f}"
        f"{rounded(v['net']):>+14,.0f}"
    )

Multiplier 2.90 instead of 1.96
4.7% of stable cells flagged significant

                erosion m3   deposition m3        net m3
slope              480,000          75,000      -400,000
calibrated         290,000          64,000      -230,000
no LoD             710,000         130,000      -580,000


Calibrated to the stable ground, the multiplier is about 2.9 instead of 1.96, which puts the LoD near 0.22 m at the region-wide NMAD. About 5% of stable cells now pass, and net lowering drops from about 400,000 to about 230,000 m3. Part 04 keeps the nominal sig_slope, so its volumes sit at the high end of this range.
This check, and the calibration itself, reuse the stable cells that the corrections and the NMAD were fit on, so they are in-sample. A held-out part of the stable ground would likely flag more.

title: 05. Simulating the storm
text:
Roughness and infiltration
Each land cover class gets a Manning’s n and an infiltration rate for unburned ground. Burned ground lost litter and duff, and severe burns can leave soil that repels water, so both values drop with burn severity. Change the numbers and rerun the cells below to see how much they matter.

# Illustrative values for unburned ground: (Manning's n, infiltration in mm/h).
unburned = {
    10: (0.40, 30.0),  # tree cover
    20: (0.30, 25.0),  # shrubland
    30: (0.20, 20.0),  # grassland
    50: (0.02, 2.0),  # built-up
    60: (0.05, 10.0),  # bare or sparse vegetation
    80: (0.04, 0.0),  # water
}
other = (0.20, 20.0)
# Illustrative multipliers by burn severity class: (Manning's n, infiltration).
severity = {1: (1.0, 1.0), 2: (0.8, 0.8), 3: (0.5, 0.5), 4: (0.3, 0.2)}


def by_class(index):
    expression = str(other[index])
    for code, values in unburned.items():
        expression = f"if(landcover == {code}, {values[index]}, {expression})"
    return expression


def by_severity(index):
    expression = "1.0"
    for code, factors in severity.items():
        expression = (
            f"if(burn_severity@PERMANENT == {code}, {factors[index]}, {expression})"
        )
    return f"if(isnull(burn_severity@PERMANENT), 1.0, {expression})"


tools.r_mapcalc(expression=f"man_prefire = {by_class(0)}")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression=f"infil_prefire = {by_class(1)}")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression=f"man_postfire = man_prefire * {by_severity(0)}")
tools.r_mapcalc(expression=f"infil_postfire = infil_prefire * {by_severity(1)}")

text:
Watch it run
Run both surfaces again with -t, which writes the discharge every 2 minutes, and play the frames over the shaded relief. In a running notebook, drag the slider or press play. The website shows the same frames as the two animations below, which play on their own.

frames, labels = {}, {}
for scenario in ("prefire", "postfire"):
    tools.g_remove(type="raster", pattern=f"q_{scenario}.*", flags="f")
    tools.r_sim_water(
        elevation="dtm_10m",
        dx="dx_10m",
        dy="dy_10m",
        rain=f"excess_{scenario}",
        man=f"man_{scenario}",
        discharge=f"q_{scenario}",
        output_step=2,
        random_seed=1,
        nprocs=4,
        flags="t",
        **{minutes: 30},
    )
    # Output steps can land a minute off, so read the names r.sim.water wrote.
    names = tools.g_list(type="raster", pattern=f"q_{scenario}.*").text.split()
    names.sort(key=lambda name: int(name.rsplit(".", 1)[1]))
    frames[scenario], labels[scenario] = [], []
    for source in names:
        minute = int(source.rsplit(".", 1)[1])
        frame = f"frame_{scenario}_{minute:02d}"
        tools.r_mapcalc(
            expression=f'{frame} = if("{source}" >= 0.05, "{source}", null())'
        )
        tools.r_colors(map=frame, rules=io.StringIO(rules))
        frames[scenario].append(frame)
        labels[scenario].append(f"{scenario}, {minute} min")


def storm_series(scenario):
    series = gj.SeriesMap(width=600, saved_region="focal@PERMANENT")
    series.d_rast(map="dtm_2022_relief")
    series.add_rasters(frames[scenario])
    series.add_vectors(
        ["mckinney_perimeter@PERMANENT"] * len(frames[scenario]),
        fill_color="none",
        color="black",
        width=2,
    )
    series.add_names(labels[scenario])
    return series

title: 05. Simulating the storm
text:
Limits

Steady rain at the peak intensity, not the storm’s three-hour hyetograph.
Roughness and infiltration are illustrative values. Calibrating them needs field measurements or a runoff record at the outlet.
A 10 m grid smooths the smallest channels.
Erosion and deposition use one set of illustrative coefficients for the whole region.

title: Geohazard Change Detection with GRASS
section: Run it on your own area
text:
Run it on your own area

Two DEMs with collection dates, from USGS 3DEP or OpenTopography
A stable mask you can defend, made of ground you expect did not change
Zones that matter to your users, such as burn severity, land cover, or subwatersheds
The chain: r.import and r.resamp.interp, t.register, r.dem.nk, r.dem.bias when you measure a bias, r.dem.lod, r.dem.change, r.dem.errprop, zonal summaries, r.dem.screen

title: Geohazard Change Detection with GRASS
text:
Three checks to carry over

Line up the grids before differencing. r.dem.dod warns you when they do not.
Report the stable-ground median and NMAD before and after every correction.
